fields.question: Why track reward saturation in SA-MRPO?
fields.answer: Already mastered objectives can crowd out unlearned dimensions. Standardize each dimension and weight by one minus saturation; the saturation estimate must be meaningful.
fields.example: If format nearly always passes, prioritize still-failing factual checks.

fields.question: How does saturation weighting differ from fixed reward weights?
fields.answer: Fixed weights ignore current mastery; saturation weighting adapts by batch. It doesn't change ultimate importance or prevent forgetting.
fields.example: After downweighting a mastered skill, keep monitoring rather than declare it permanently solved.

fields.question: Can SA-MRPO compute one saturation after aggregating rewards?
fields.answer: No. That removes per-dimension budget allocation. Track each mean, variance and saturation before aggregation. Candidate formulas don't reproduce checkpoint training.
fields.example: One aggregate hides low correctness and high format performance.

fields.question: Why adjust weights based on saturation instead of always treating objectives equally?
fields.answer: Mastered dimensions can waste budget needed elsewhere. Normalize per dimension, then reduce saturated goals by a specified statistic. High scores don't mean permanent mastery, and raw scale isn't mastery.
fields.example: Reduce formatting pressure if already solved, but check whether later reasoning training degrades it.

fields.question: Why randomly hide rubric criteria?
fields.answer: Fixed proxies can be repeatedly exploited. Random subsets make a single shortcut unreliable. Hidden criteria are not unimportant; the visible reward composition changes during training.
fields.example: A canned phrase cannot reliably earn total reward if its easy criterion is often absent.

fields.question: How does group-shared dropout differ from independent masks per response?
fields.answer: A shared subset keeps same-prompt responses comparable. Independent masks confound quality with scoring criteria. Randomize by group.
fields.example: Comparing A on format and B on correctness doesn't isolate answer quality.

fields.question: When should Rubric Dropout sample and save the mask?
fields.answer: Sample one mask per rollout group, freeze for scoring and log seed. Never choose masks after seeing which response benefits. No local real rubric judge.
fields.example: Hiding difficult criteria only after observing failure is cherry-picking, not dropout.

fields.question: Why share a rubric subset within a rollout group?
fields.answer: Relative rewards need common criteria; different random criteria can misrank peers. Cross-group randomization reduces fixed shortcuts, but doesn't guarantee valid remaining criteria or protect task performance.
fields.example: Omit brevity for both answers, not only one.

fields.question: Why derive RRC generative reward from relative ranking?
fields.answer: Generative judges may compare reliably without calibrated standalone scores. Within-group ranks plus anchors yield centered rewards while exploiting comparative strength.
fields.example: A judge may prefer one summary reliably but inconsistently use a ten-point scale.

fields.question: What do group self-competition and anchor ranks each provide?
fields.answer: Group comparisons separate current candidates; anchors bridge groups where ranks alone hide absolute level. Specify weights; rank gaps aren't equal quality distances.
fields.example: An all-bad group still has a winner; an anchor can show it remains poor.

fields.question: Why check group size and rank direction before converting RRC ranks to rewards?
fields.answer: K−1 requires more than one sample. Declare whether rank one is best. No local real judging or complete capability integration.
fields.example: A reversed formula can give the best rank the lowest reward.

fields.question: Why combine group and anchor ranking rather than ask for absolute scores?
fields.answer: Comparative judgments can be more stable than absolute scale. Group competition gives relative position; anchors give cross-group reference before centering. This still depends on candidates and judge, not absolute truth or full paper evaluation.
fields.example: Two group winners may have very different quality relative to a shared anchor.

fields.question: Why not simply trust high privileged-teacher confidence in ADRS?
fields.answer: Extra skills/context may boost confidence without returns. Gate dense feedback by correlation between same-step teacher scores and observed returns.
fields.example: A teacher can favor a tool action that frequently fails.

fields.question: How does TVA correlation gating differ from fixed distillation weight?
fields.answer: Fixed weight always trusts teacher; positive correlation retains signals associated with returns. Batch correlation is not causality and may not use test gold.
fields.example: If teacher scores don't track success, extra guidance weakens.

fields.question: Does ADRS standardize over a full trajectory or within interaction steps?
fields.answer: Standardize teacher scores within each interaction step and correlate across trajectory returns, then feed host reward-to-advantage logic. Local z-scores aren't correctness labels.
fields.example: Compare second tool calls with other second calls, not every turn combined.

fields.question: Why check teacher confidence against realized return before using token guidance?
fields.answer: Privileged certainty can amplify error. Normalize within interaction steps, gate by positive return association and use the existing reward-to-advantage path. Negative association isn't help; inference does not use privileged training skill/outcome.
fields.example: Gate out confidence in fluent but ineffective tool calls.

fields.question: Why keep a Good–Normal–Bad archive in SERPO?
fields.answer: Different qualities inform prompt-specific rubrics and policy learning. Actor and criteria evolve; storing only highest scores loses contrasts. Classification depends on judge quality.
fields.example: Medium answers expose gaps and bad answers show patterns to avoid.

fields.question: How does SERPO differ from repeated RL under a fixed rubric?
fields.answer: It updates query-specific rubrics and archives with the actor. Fixed criteria can lose discrimination, but coevolution risks drift and self-reinforcement. Self-scores aren't proof.
fields.example: New criteria can distinguish harder negatives after the actor learns initial rules.

fields.question: How should SERPO track its three evolving states?
fields.answer: Record versions and ordering of generation, archive, rubric and actor updates. Don't retrospectively score with later rubrics. Local candidates don't implement full generation/judging.
fields.example: Log the actual rubric used for each batch so training supervision is auditable.

fields.question: Why separate SERPO archive, rubric and actor roles?
fields.answer: The archive stores comparisons, rubric defines current standards, and actor generates. Feedback can adapt or amplify bias. New archive or rubric doesn't itself train or improve the model; use independent holdout.
fields.example: A short-only archive, brevity rubric and short actor may agree while neglecting facts.

fields.question: Why replay one reply with and without criteria in CoRT?
fields.answer: Keep response fixed so likelihood differences link rubric context to token positions, redistributing response advantage rather than adding another global score.
fields.example: A format requirement can affect bracket tokens and their credit.

fields.question: How does CoRT counterfactual replay differ from attention weighting?
fields.answer: Replay changes evaluation context and compares probabilities; attention measures one forward's information weights. Neither directly proves causality; attention isn't the specified contrast.
fields.example: A high-attention token may show unchanged likelihood when criteria are removed.

fields.question: Why align both CoRT scoring passes to the same token and prefix?
fields.answer: Different generated text confounds the criteria intervention. Normalized weights scale fixed advantage; original student sampling must not see the privileged rubric. Candidate features aren't token replay.
fields.example: Scoring sentence A with criteria and B without doesn't isolate their effect.

fields.question: Why replay the same response instead of generating separately under each rubric view?
fields.answer: Fixed tokens/prefixes isolate conditioning better; regenerating also changes trajectories. Use the difference to allocate original advantage, not pass scoring text into deployment. Counterfactual contexts can still bias the estimate.
fields.example: A citation token's likelihood can change with a citation requirement; regenerating the whole paragraph adds other changes.
